title-group.article-title: Effects of perioperative application of esketamine on postpartum depression in cesarean section: A systematic review and meta-analysis

sec.title: Background:
sec.p: To evaluate the effect of perioperative esketamine administration on postpartum depression in pregnant women undergoing cesarean section.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: Data sources was PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library from inception to February 1, 2024. Randomized controlled trials in pregnant women undergoing cesarean section were selected and compared to the use of esketamine in the perioperative period. The primary outcome measure was the incidence of postpartum maternal depression. Preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used. Data pooled by random-effects models are presented as risk ratios (RR) (95% confidence intervals, 95% CI) or mean differences (95% CI). This review was registered in PROSPERO (ID: CRD42023431197).

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: We included 8 studies with a total of 1655 participants. The quality of the studies was rated high or unclear. Seven studies involving 1485 participants reported the incidence of postpartum depression. Compared with pregnant women undergoing cesarean section without the use of esketamine, those using esketamine in the perioperative period showed a 48% decreased risk of developing postpartum depression (RR: 0.52, 95% CI: 0.35–0.79) and a 1.43-point reduction in EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale) (mean difference: −1.43, 95% CI: −2.32 to −0.54). For immediate intraoperative adverse reactions, the application of esketamine caused maternal nausea and vomiting (RR: 2.16, 95% CI: 1.22–3.81), dizziness (RR: 6.11, 95% CI: 1.49–24.98), and hallucinations (RR: 6.83, 95% CI: 1.57–29.68) compared to no esketamine use.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Perioperative use of esketamine in pregnant women undergoing cesarean section may reduce postpartum depression and increase intraoperative adverse reactions, but has no significant effect on postoperative adverse reactions.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a disabling but treatable mental disorder that is one of the most common complications of childbearing.[1] The American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, fifth edition defines PPD as a major depressive episode “with peripartum onset” and elaborates, “if onset of mood symptoms occurs during pregnancy or in the 4 weeks following delivery.” However, in clinical practice and research, PPD is variably defined as occurring from 4 weeks to 12 months after childbirth. The estimated prevalence of PPD ranges from 6.9% to 12.9% in high-income countries and more than 20% in some low- or middle-income countries.[2] Symptoms of PPD often include sleep disturbance, anxiety, irritability, a feeling of being overwhelmed, and obsessional worries or preoccupation, often about the baby’s health, feeding, and bathing safety. Approximately 20% of women with PPD symptoms experience suicidal thoughts.[1] Timely detection and management of this group of patients is particularly important.

Effective management of PPD requires a comprehensive and often multidisciplinary approach, including psychosocial, psychological, and pharmacological interventions. Whether it is a psychosocial or pharmacological intervention, the onset of action does not meet the requirements of dealing with acute events (e.g., suicide). The latest treatment for PPD is an injectable drug called brexanolone, which has a price of about US $35,000 and requires inpatient care for 60 hours for drug infusion (with the hospital stay, naturally, adding to the costs).[3] Its advantages and disadvantages are obvious; it produces antidepressant effects quickly, but is expensive.

Innovative treatments in psychiatry are rare enough for any new developments to be applauded. Therefore, esketamine (a narcotic analgesic that has shown good efficacy in the management of treatment-resistant depression (TRD) has come to the fore. Two randomized control trials have shown that intravenous or intranasal esketamine produces rapid antidepressant effects in patients with TRD.[4,5] Research on the therapeutic and preventive effects of esketamine in PPD is gradually increasing. Controversy exists between studies, and a systematic review and meta-analysis are necessary.

sec.title: 2. Methods
sec.p: We developed and followed a protocol for all steps of our systematic review and meta-analysis (Appendix S1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N135). The study was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis guidelines.

sec.title: 2.1. Literature search and inclusion criteria
sec.p: We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library from inception to February 1, 2024, for potentially relevant studies using the search terms Depression, Postpartum and Cesarean Section (Mesh), and esketamine (Mesh). Appendix S2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N136, provides full details of the search strategy. Additionally, we manually searched the reference lists of the included articles.

We considered studies eligible for inclusion if they were randomized controlled trials including pregnant women undergoing cesarean section with perioperative use of esketamine, reported incidence of PPD or postpartum EDPS scores and adverse reactions, and included a comparator of women undergoing cesarean section with perioperative use of saline or other analgesics. Studies were excluded if they lacked relevant data on the PPD outcomes. Publications without original data, such as reviews, editorials, and comments, were also excluded. The study selection was performed in 2 phases: primary screening of titles and abstracts, followed by a full-text review of potentially eligible articles. Two review authors (BM and XT) independently evaluated eligibility, with discrepancies resolved by a third investigator (SW).

sec.title: 2.2. Data extraction and outcome assessments
sec.p: Two authors (BM and XT) independently extracted data from eligible studies using piloted data-extraction sheets. Extracted data included the first author, year of publication, country where the study was conducted, total number of people included in the study, baseline information, interventions, comparators, observed indicators of follow-up time, and diagnostic criteria.

The primary outcome was the incidence of PPD. Secondary outcomes were postpartum Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) scores and adverse reactions (adverse reactions during the operation: nausea and vomiting, dizziness, hallucinations; adverse reactions after operation, nausea and vomiting, dizziness, pruritus).

sec.title: 2.3. Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: Two reviewers (BM and XT) independently assessed the risk of bias of selected studies according to the Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for randomized controlled trials (risk of bias).[6] The following characteristics were evaluated: random sequence generation (selection bias), allocation concealment (selection bias), blinding of participants and personnel (performance bias), blinding of outcome assessment (detection bias), incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), selective reporting (reporting bias) and other biases. The results of these questions were graphed and assessed using Review Manager 5.4. Two reviewers (BM and XT) rated the risk for each item as low, unclear, or high. Appendix S3, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N137, provides a detailed description and decision criteria for each item in the risk of bias. A senior investigator (SW) resolved these discrepancies.

sec.title: 2.4. Data synthesis and analysis
sec.p: The extracted data for the meta-analysis were analyzed using Review Manager 5.4. The P values were 2-sided, with an α level of 0.05 considered significant. A random-effects model was used to calculate pooled risk ratios with 95% confidence intervals for the incidence of PPD and adverse reactions, and was used to calculate weighted mean differences with 95% confidence intervals for the EPDS score. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I2 statistic. To identify the subgroup differences and potential sources of the observed heterogeneity, we carried out subgroup analyses after stratifying for diagnostic methods (specialist involvement or specialist not involvement); dosage (≤0.5 or >0.5 mg/kg); intervention (intravenous injection [IV] or patient-controlled intravenous analgesia [PCIA]).

sec.title: 2.5. Data synthesis and analysis
sec.p: No patients or members of the public were directly involved in the development or completion of this study, owing to time and funding constraints. However, the greatest impetus for completing this study was the research team’s keen interest in whether perioperative use of esketamine would prevent the onset of PPD.

sec.title: 3.1. Study selection, characteristics, and quality assessment
sec.p: In our initial search, we identified 51 records after removing duplicates and indices. The full text of the 14 articles was subsequently reviewed based on screening of titles and abstract reviews. Eight studies with 1655 participants were eligible for data extraction and quantitative analysis.[7–14] Figure 1 shows the flow of records throughout the review. Appendix S4, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N138, includes a list of excluded studies with reasons for exclusion, and Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N129, and Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N130, summarize the characteristics of the included articles. The included studies were based on 4 datasets published between 2022 and 2024. Seven studies reported assessments of maternal postpartum depressive status, and all studies reported assessments of adverse reactions, with 4 studies reporting postpartum EPDS scores.[8,10,12,14] Most studies used EPDS scores to define the diagnosis of PPD, and only 2 studies[7,12] reported a diagnosis with professional physician involvement (involvement made the diagnosis more definitive).

caption.p: Literature flowchart. PRISMA = Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis.

sec.p: Of the 1485 women who underwent cesarean section, 221 were diagnosed with PPD. Of the 667 patients who did not receive perioperative esketamine intervention, 130 experienced PPD. PPD was diagnosed in 91 of 818 mothers treated with prophylactic esketamine administration in the perioperative period. Table S1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N129, summarizes the outcomes of this study. Table S2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N130, presents the baseline personal and demographic characteristics of the 2 groups. According to the risk of bias tool, most studies were judged to have a low risk of bias, while 1 study[7] considered an unclear risk of bias. Figure S1, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N132, and Table S3, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N131, present detailed assessments of the risk of bias for each domain.

sec.title: 3.2. Primary outcomes: incidence of PPD
sec.p: Seven studies with 1485 participants reported the incidence of PPD.[7–13] All 7 studies reported the incidence of PPD in the short-term postpartum period (≤7 days) and longer postpartum period (≥28 days). Compared with maternal cesarean section without the use of esketamine, maternal cesarean section with esketamine in the perioperative period showed a 48% decreased risk of developing PPD in the longer postpartum period (RR: 0.52, 95% CI: 0.35–0.79, I2 = 55%) (Fig. 2A) and a 59% decreased risk of developing PPD in the short-term postpartum period (RR: 0.41, 95% CI: 0.26–0.66, I2 = 54%) (Fig. 2B).

caption.p: Risk ratios for PPD in pregnant women undergoing cesarean section with or without using of esketamine. CI = confidence interval, PPD = postpartum depression.

sec.title: 3.3. Secondary outcome: postpartum EPDS scores and incidence of adverse reactions
sec.p: Four studies containing 863 participants reported EPDS at various times during the postpartum period (short-term postpartum period: ≤7 days; longer postpartum period: ≥28 days). Perioperative administration of esketamine in women undergoing cesarean section showed lower EPDS scores than those receiving other analgesics or saline (≤7 days: mean differences: −1.43, 95% CI: −2.32 to −0.54, I2 = 79%; ≥28 days: −0.62, 95% CI: −1.33, 0.09, I2 = 63%) (Fig. 3A, B). All included studies reported adverse reactions during dosing, both during intraoperative and postoperative dosing. During intraoperative medication, esketamine increased maternal nausea and vomiting (RR: 2.16, 95% CI: 1.22–3.81, I2 = 35%), dizziness (RR: 6.11, 95% CI: 1.49–24.98; I2 = 79%), and hallucinations (RR: 6.83, 95% CI: 1.57–29.68; I2 = 0%) (Fig. 4A–C). The use of esketamine reduced maternal nausea and vomiting (RR: 0.62, 95% CI: 0.41–0.92, I2 = 36%) during the postoperative medication period, but had no significant effect on postoperative dizziness (RR: 1.95, 95% CI: 0.52–7.27, I2 = 76%) and pruritus (RR: 0.31, 95% CI: 0.07–1.31, I2 = 0%) compared with the control group (Figure S2, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N133).

caption.p: EPDS in pregnant women undergoing cesarean section with or without using of esketamine. CI = confidence interval, SD = standard deviation, EPDS = Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, IV = intravenous injection, PPD = postpartum depression.
Risk ratios for intraoperative adverse reactions. CI = confidence interval.

sec.title: 3.4. Subgroup analysis
sec.p: To investigate the presence of subgroup differences in the outcome of PPD in the longer postpartum period, we conducted a subgroup analysis according to the characteristics of eligible studies, including diagnostic methods, intervention, and dosage. Interestingly, changes in diagnostic modalities (specialist involvement: RR: 0.55, 95% CI: 0.08–3.59, I2 = 53%; specialist not involvement: RR: 0.53, 95% CI: 0.34–0.83, I2 = 55%) and esketamine administration (IV: RR: 0.59, 95% CI:0.29–1.21; I2 = 30%; PCIA: RR: 0.52, 95% CI: 0.35–0.79, I2 = 70%) affected the incidence of PPD over the longer postpartum period (Figure S3, Supplemental Digital Content, http://links.lww.com/MD/N134).

sec.title: 4.1. Principal findings
sec.p: The findings of this systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies suggest that the perioperative prophylactic use of esketamine reduced the risk of maternal PPD and decreased EPDS scores, but increased adverse drug reactions during the medication period. These findings indicate the feasibility of perioperative use of esketamine to prevent PPD onset.

sec.title: 4.2. Choice of outcomes
sec.p: The timing of PPD assessment varied among the included studies. According to the definition of PPD, the incidence of PPD during the longer postpartum period (≥28 days) after delivery was selected as the primary outcome. We also obtained the incidence of short-term PPD (≤7 days). When extracting the EPDS, the same principles as described above were followed. The other outcome of the study was adverse reactions, which varied from study to study; we selected the adverse reaction profile to reflect safety in 2 different periods of medication. During intraoperative medication administration, we extracted data from 4 studies, mainly concerning nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, and dizziness. During the postoperative medication period, we extracted data from 8 studies, mainly concerning nausea and vomiting, dizziness, and pruritus.

According to the results of our study, esketamine increased adverse maternal effects (including nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, and dizziness) during intraoperative administration. Based on medication experience, adverse reactions to esketamine are transient, and the adverse reactions manifested by intravenous injection and slow small-dose intravenous pumping (for example, in the case of PCIA) are different. Therefore, the assessment and combination of adverse reactions should be standardized and clarified. Future research should clarify the time point for assessment and how a balance can be achieved between adverse drug reactions and the benefits of drug application, which can be achieved by further assessing satisfaction with anesthesia and analgesia.

sec.title: 4.3. Implications of subgroup analyses
sec.p: Prior to data processing, 3 subgroups were predefined: diagnostic methods (specialist involvement or specialist not involvement), dosage (≤0.5 or >0.5 mg/kg), and intervention (IV or PCIA). The diagnosis of PPD is one of the major difficulties in this field, and the involvement of a psychologist or psychiatrist can lead to a better judgment. Based on the results of this study, the involvement of a specialized physician affects the primary outcome. The current study emphasizes the risk of PPD[8] rather than the diagnosis of PPD, which is the best approach in the field of clinical research.

Considering that a higher dose of esketamine increases its adverse reactions, we used 0.5 mg/kg as the dividing line and divided it into a low-dose group and a high-dose group. However, we found that regardless of whether it is a low-dose or high-dose subgroup, the application of esketamine can reduce the occurrence of PPD. This is interesting, and considering the heterogeneity between the incorporated studies, this issue needs further validation.

In the current study, most of the interventions were performed by adding esketamine to postoperative analgesia, probably because of the ease and feasibility of implementing this intervention over intraoperative intravenous pumping of esketamine. The incidence of immediate adverse reactions to intraoperative pumped esketamine is extremely high; during the intraoperative period, more patients administered esketamine developed neurological or mental symptoms (97.7% [293 of 300]) compared with the placebo group (4.7% [14 of 300]; P < .001).[15] The results of the present study similarly showed that nausea and vomiting, hallucinations, and dizziness were more likely to occur in laboring women administered intraoperative intravenous esketamine. However, these reactions are transient. During the first postoperative day, mental symptoms did not differ between the esketamine and placebo.[15] We then grouped the 2 modes of administration and found that the IV group did not reduce the risk of PPD, whereas the PCIA group reduced the occurrence of PPD. The mechanism underlying this and feasibility of the results need to be corroborated by more relevant clinical studies. In summary, the subgroup differences highlighted the need for high-quality studies on efficacy and safety, specifically the improvement in standardization of PPD diagnosis and accuracy of the assessment of adverse reactions to fill the gaps in evidence.

sec.title: 4.4. Potential underlying mechanisms
sec.p: The population included in this study consisted of pregnant women who underwent cesarean section and did not opt for spontaneous delivery (including painless delivery). This is because studies have found that the incidence of PPD is higher in cesarean sections than in normal deliveries.[16] Pain stimulation is an important cause of maternal mood changes, and ketamine may have a dual effect of reducing pain and directly reducing depressive symptoms. Ketamine and its enantiomers (including esketamine and arketamine) have each demonstrated distinct antidepressant effects.[4,17] It is worth noting that in addition to the current esketamine, which has published clinical trial results,[4] some data from the phase II clinical trial of arketamine have also given promising results.[18] This study showed a significant reduction in depressive symptoms, improvement in social and occupational functioning, and a reduction in sick leave and hospitalization after a single dose of arketamine in 3 patients with TRD.[18] Compared to arketamine, esketamine has a higher affinity for N-methyl-d-aspartate receptors (NMDAR),[19] which may have contributed to the earlier development and use of esketamine. Among the many disorders with depressive symptoms, in the case of PPD, the use of ketamine has been shown to reduce the occurrence of PPD in previous studies. However, extension of use was hampered by its psychoneurological side effects and the need for hospitalization.[20] The current study showed transient intraoperative elevation in various psychoneurological symptom side effects with low doses of esketamine compared with controls, but no significant difference in the postoperative period.[15] As the study did not assess overall anesthesia satisfaction, it did not provide a good indication of the trade-off between effectiveness and safety. If the benefits of esketamine outweigh its side effects, it would be a good choice. Studies have shown that ketamine and esketamine exert their antidepressant effects by acting on NMDA receptors to modulate neuronal activity and synaptic plasticity.[21,22] Interestingly, arketamine, which does not have a high affinity for NDMAR, also demonstrated excellent antidepressant effects, suggesting that the mechanism of the antidepressant effect needs to be further explored, which was found to be possibly related to brain-derived neurotrophic factor.[23,24] As esketamine continues to be used, concerns about adverse drug reactions are emerging, especially regarding long-term efficacy, addiction risks, and suicidal risks.[25,26] These concerns suggest that esketamine is a double-edged sword, capable of being antidepressant by acting on NMDAR and also producing corresponding psychiatric symptomatic side effects via NMDAR. This evidence suggests that although the current studies basically express a good preventive effect, a long research journey is needed to prove and confirm the effectiveness and safety of esketamine. For the time being, esketamine can be used as a prophylactic, short-term, and adjunctive medication to combat depressive symptoms. Meanwhile, we are also looking forward to phase II clinical data on arketamine, as it can be found that arketamine seems to have lower psychiatric symptomatic side effects.[17,18]

sec.title: 4.5. Limitations of this study
sec.p: Our study has some limitations. First, the comparison measures, data materials, and quality of the studies varied; thus, the high heterogeneity indicates that our results need to be confirmed by additional high-quality studies. Second, the key information on PPD diagnosis and follow-up duration varied between studies and lacked standardization. Hence, the standard diagnostic principles and precise time course of the effects of esketamine on PPD need to be evaluated. Third, EPDS scores were not captured in 4 studies, which reduced the sample size for assessing EPDS scores. Finally, subgroup analysis did not address the high heterogeneity among the studies. Therefore, new original high-quality studies with diagnostic criteria are needed to investigate the feasibility of esketamine for the prevention and treatment of PPD.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: Our systematic review and meta-analysis showed that perioperative use of esketamine may reduce the risk of PPD in mothers who have undergone cesarean section. These results need to be interpreted with caution, and uncertainties need to be confirmed by further studies.
